sessions.feedback: The screen's 1d % is not dividend-adjusted, so closed-end funds going ex-dividend (GAM -12%, CET -6.6%) show up as top 'unusual moves'. Flagging ex-dividend dates, or adjusting for them, would save research budget. The earnings column also only says 'time not given', and consensus EPS or revenue figures would help with the surprise direction. Nothing blocked a trade this session.
Nothing blocking. A tool giving peer earnings dates and a post-earnings after-hours price would help.

The web_search result inside code_execution came back as a JSON string, so it had to be parsed with json.loads. Search results for specific recent news are poor and often years old. A direct news-by-ticker tool would help.
web_search in code_execution returns a JSON string rather than a list, which is not obvious from the docs. The digest has no pre-market prices for all names, but otherwise nothing held me back.

summary:
Session 2026-11-17.

Session 2026-11-17. ECPG settled earlier (stopped out, -12.4%). Market: SPY -1.9%, Nasdaq -2.5% on 11-16 (AI/chip selloff, NVDA leadership turmoil, new chip-export rule, yields >5%). NVDA reports after the close today, a binary event. Pre-market is flat to slightly up, and China ADRs are weak (BABA -3%).

Decisions:
1) Closed UNM short (-5.3%). The bad-news drift failed: the stock bounced about 5% off its post-gap close and held up as a defensive name in the selloff, and analyst targets (MS 85, WF 91) sit above the price.
2) Extended FIS short 5 more trading days (stop +10%, target -12%, p=0.52). It sits near its 52w low and the drift is slow, with squeeze risk if the market rebounds on NVDA.

Passed: HTHT (beat and raise +8.9%, but the China ADR tape is weak and the August pop faded), TSN (earnings gap-up fading pre-market), MOH/CNC/ELV (defensive rotation, giving back pre-market), TU (Quebecor takeover proposal, deal-driven), CRTO (MSCI inclusion run-up already +17%), small caps OFRM/BGIN/MFI (costly slippage). GAM and CET looked like -12% and -6.6% drops, but they were closed-end fund ex-dividend dates (screen not dividend-adjusted). HD/VIK/JD/DIS report this morning with moderate pre-market moves and no consensus figures in hand. Book is about 5.7% short, about 94% cash.

Next session: FIS horizon is now about 11-24. Watch the NVDA reaction, since a rebound hurts the short. BABA/PDD earnings are 11-19. Look for post-NVDA overreaction setups, and check ex-dividend dates before trusting any no-news drop.
notes:
NOTES (updated 2026-11-17)

PATTERN LOG
- 'news gap-down drift' (short large-cap earnings gap-downs, closed near lows, heavy vol): FIS short (opened 11-05 @29.75; ~-5% by 11-16, drift small, stock stabilised 28-30 after day 1), UNM short (opened 11-05 @74.72; stock bounced +5% from post-gap close, defensive insurer outperformed in an AI/tech selloff -> thesis invalid, closed 11-17). Lesson: after the first 1-2 days the drift is tiny; the day-0 gap contains most of it. Defensive/low-beta names can rally when the market sells off, so a short on a low-beta stock is secretly a bet that the market rebounds.
- 'news gap-up drift': ECPG long 11-06 -> stopped out -12.4% (-13.1 vs SPY). Peer PRAA -37% on its own earnings the next day crushed it. Lesson: check peer/sector earnings before buying a gap-up, and gap-up longs bought the day after are chasing.
- Screen history stats are noisy: news-driven rows go on 45-60% of time; no pattern has a robust edge yet. Don't force trades; 2 sessions in a row with no good setup.

DATA TRAPS
- Screen's 1d % is NOT dividend-adjusted. GAM (-12%) and CET (-6.6%) on 11-16 were just ex-dividend dates ($7.43 and $3.00 year-end distributions) of closed-end funds. Check ex-div before treating a no-news drop as a reversal candidate.
- Pre-market prints on <1% of avg volume are noise.
- web_search in code_execution returns JSON string (json.loads) and items are dicts only after parsing.

MARKET CONTEXT (Nov 2026)
- 11-05 SPY -4.4% intraday crash (index ~733), rebounds 11-09 (+2.4%), then 11-13/11-16 slide: SPY 739.95 on 11-16 (-1.9%), Nasdaq -2.5% (correction), AI-chip selloff, NVDA leadership turmoil (Huang exit), new US chip-export rule, Treasury yields >5%. NVDA earnings after close 11-17 (binary). Fed: Warsh is Chair; Fed speakers all week.
- 11-16 defensive rotation: managed care (MOH +11%, CNC +5%, ELV +4%), utilities, food names rallied on a down day; pre-market 11-17 they give back 1-3%.
- TU (TELUS) +12% on Quebecor C$/US$21.7B takeover proposal (jumped 29% intraday then pared) - deal-news, not traded.
- China ADRs weak (BABA -4% and -3% pre-mkt, BIDU -5%); BABA/PDD earnings 11-19 pre-open.

PASSED ON 11-17: HTHT (beat+raise +8.9%, but China ADR tape weak, Aug-17 pop faded within weeks, thin edge), TSN (+8.7% earnings, pre-market fading, FY27 sales guide down), MOH/CNC/ELV (sector defensive rotation), CRTO (MSCI inclusion 11-30 run-up already +17%), OFRM/BGIN/MFI (small, costly), TPB (-66% from high, 8-day streak, momentum not reversal), HD/VIK/JD/DIS (earnings pre-open, pre-market moves modest, no consensus numbers in hand).

OPEN IDEAS
- Index-inclusion run-up/reversal around MSCI effective date (CRTO 11-30).
- Test whether stocks that bounce after a first-day gap-down (UNM) keep bouncing.

prompt:
Your universe is every eligible US stock, long or short. You have one goal: exploit sudden price moves
and recurring market patterns aggressively and cleverly. How you do that is up to you.

Each morning you get a screen of the last session's most unusual moves among all eligible stocks:
each move in units of the stock's own volatility and net of its industry, volume against its
average, the gap, where it closed in its range, the run-up before, the 52-week range, pre-market
trading, news stories and earnings. The scan tool gives the same row for any ticker, so check peers,
suppliers and sympathy moves. Below the screen, code shows how each pattern you have named has done
and how earlier screen rows moved afterwards.

What published research says. Test it; your own record counts for more:
- Big moves with no identifiable news have tended to partly reverse over days to a few weeks. Moves
  backed by real information (earnings, guidance, analyst changes, deals) have tended to keep
  drifting, bad news especially. The reversal is cleaner measured against the industry and in stocks
  whose volume did not explode; heavy volume has tended to mean continuation.
- Stocks bought heavily by retail traders on attention spikes have tended to fall back over the
  following weeks.
- You fill at the open. Overnight moves have tended to carry on through the open and fade during the
  day, so buying a hyped gap-up at the open is a poor entry, and a pre-market that has already undone
  the move leaves little to take.
- Reversal trades pay for providing liquidity, and pay best when markets are stressed. They fail when
  the move had news, when the whole industry moved, and in sharp rebounds after a sell-off, when
  shorting the losers hurts most. Crowded shorts can squeeze.
- Many patterns weakened after they were published, and smaller stocks cost more to trade here: a
  round trip is about 0.2% in large caps and 1% in the smallest.

How to work:
- Start from the screen. Take the rows that look most mispriced, find out why each moved (read the
  news, check the earnings date and the pre-market), and decide what is left to take at the open.
- Be aggressive when the evidence lines up: size up, short spikes you can explain, run several
  positions on a busy day. Doing nothing because you did not look is the failure this agent exists to
  avoid. When you pass, say in your summary which rows you examined and why each was not a trade.
- Every trade names its pattern, says why the price is wrong and what would prove you wrong, and has
  an exit. Reuse a pattern's name whenever you trade the same idea, so its record builds up.
- Set stops for the pattern: a reversal needs room to work, so a stop inside the stock's normal daily
  range mostly sells the bounce. Size by how volatile the stock is.
- Keep a pattern log in your notes: what each pattern is, the trades behind it, how they did against
  SPY, and whether you still believe it. Trust the code-written records over your memory. Drop what
  keeps losing and try new patterns you spot.
